comments.text:
So what to buy? I went with an A770 16GB between the options that I could actually buy today at MSRP. Versus the 6600XT and 3060 it wins. I think it's that simple.

If you open up the comparison to a 6700XT and 3060 Ti though, things change a bit. The problem is availability and getting MSRP pricing. If you can get an A770 on Newegg, it's always MSRP.
The 6700XT would be a better choice if you can get it, and at MSRP. The 6700XT with its mix of performance and 12GB is probably the best card in this price range. The NV cards do have good RT and DLSS but I'm not sure how I feel about 8GB today. The 3060 12GB is beaten by 20% or so by the A770. Midrange isn't fast enough for RT at 4K, but 4K at less than 10GB will choke performance even further in AAA games. These cards can do 4K with options turned down. Reviewers make it seem like you need a 4090 to get games to run at all.

Arc A770: the RAM, the RT, but missing optimization. 
Geforce 3060 Ti: missing the RAM, the RT, best optimized (debatable though as AMD has made major strides here, I'd consider them on nearly equal footing).
Radeon 6700XT: the RAM, enough raw perf to make up for weaker RT at 1080P at least, well optimized. This is one of my favorite cards on the market.

I stand by the A770 over 3060 8/12GB and 6600XT. That's the comparison Intel intended and it is favorable IMO once you consider everything. I think Intel has a strong product on their hands considering the market if you go looking for a GPU. They definitely couldn't wait any longer to launch it than they did but the market is still pretty rough. I'm glad I picked up an Arc when I did.

I actually would like you guys to test installing the Windows version of DXVK (you know, the DirectX-to-Vulkan translation layer Valve uses for Proton on the Steam Deck) on the older games and compare it against Intel's driver-level emulation of those graphics APIs.

DX12 and Vulkan grant games much lower level access to the GPU than prior APIs (much like Glide used to do for 3dfx accelerators in the 90s). This means that for those new APIs, GPUs and their drivers can get away with being significantly dumber and relying on the game engines' own decision-making. For DX11, OpenGL and below however, the driver and GPU have to make more decisions about how they're going to go about rendering the scenes.

Just like the Intel drivers, DXVK is concerned with this obstacle when it works translating older DirectX titles to Vulkan. So, is it faster to let DXVK handle older APIs on Arc for the time being until Intel is done optimizing their drivers?

comments.text:
Yea so all these very modern games, it works on. But it's gonna be a nightmare to run these cards if you enjoy older games. With no native DX9 or older support, and very fresh drivers.. They just aren't going to work. Even the decade old integrated intel GPUs still have tons of problems with older DX9 cards, and they have native support. DX9on12 or other wrappers work in some games, but not all, and often lead to glitches that are sometimes fixable with various tweaks, but not something your average gamer is gonna want to troubleshoot through. So yea, unless you ONLY plan to play brand new games, i'd not recommend this for a long time until DX9on12, and intels drivers, are actually proven to work decently on older titles.

Plus the fact it relies so heavily on DX12 to win against the RTx3060 is also problmatic as digital foundry has shown time and time again, DX12 is still very much a beta API. Hundreds of games, including every UE4 title with DX12 support all have shader compilation stuttering, which is far less noticable on DX11. Some games it downright unplayable on DX12 in some configurations, eg: FF7 remake, especially on sub 10GB card. So for the here and now, DX11 wins, and plenty of very epic games, and even still many multiplayer ones with online community still very active today run on DX9 and DX11 predominantly. Vulkan is in general a big improvement over OpenGL, no major downsides other than issues with various overlays/injectors, mostly applies to the most hardcore gamers who enjoy tools like SpecialK. (SpecialK can semi support vulkan, but not display it's overlay).
